clinical: Psoriasis
In psoriasis, keratinocytes are made far faster than normal, so the epidermis thickens and the outer layer stays scaly and keeps its nuclei (parakeratosis).
Bullous pemphigoid

Autoantibodies attack the hemidesmosome proteins (BP180 and BP230) that anchor basal cells to the basement membrane. The epidermis then splits from the dermis and forms tense blisters, mostly in older adults.

Epidermis – cellular field.description: Keratinocytes, the main cells of the epidermis, mature as they move from the basal layer to the surface. They divide at the bottom, fill with keratin and keratohyalin granules, and finally die as flat, horny cells. Melanocytes sit among the basal cells and pass melanin to nearby keratinocytes, which shades the nucleus against UV light.
clinical: Melanoma
Malignant melanoma arises from melanocytes, often after intense UV exposure. The ABCDE rule (asymmetry, irregular border, colour variation, diameter over 6 mm, evolving shape) helps spot it early.
Filaggrin and skin barrier

Filaggrin, released from keratohyalin granules, binds keratin filaments and helps keep the outer skin hydrated. Loss-of-function mutations in its gene cause ichthyosis vulgaris and raise the risk of atopic dermatitis.

Dermis – retained context.description: The deeper, thicker part of the dermis, made of dense irregular connective tissue rich in type I collagen. It gives the skin its strength and stretch resistance and carries the hair follicles, sweat glands, vessels and nerves.
clinical: Keloid
Keloids form when the dermis lays down excess collagen after injury, producing raised scars that grow beyond the original wound edge.
Stretch marks
Stretch marks (striae) appear when rapid stretching tears the collagen and elastic fibres of the dermis, leaving pale streaks.

Tissue restoration covers.description: The dermis and the fatty hypodermis form the outer covering over the hair follicles, glands and vessels. The reticular dermis is dense connective tissue rich in type I collagen, and the hypodermis below is white fat divided into lobules by fibrous septa.

Hypodermis – bulk context.description: The hypodermis is the layer of white fat beneath the dermis, divided into lobules by fibrous septa. The septa tie the skin to the deep fascia and carry the larger vessels and nerves, while the fat insulates, cushions and stores energy.
clinical: Lipoma
A lipoma is a common, benign tumour of mature fat cells that forms a soft, movable lump in the subcutaneous fat.

Cell-field restoration covers.description: This group contains the cells of the epidermis and of the fat layer. Keratinocytes make keratin and form most of the epidermis, melanocytes make the pigment melanin, and adipocytes are large fat cells that store energy in a single lipid droplet.

Hypodermis – unilocular cell field.description: Adipocytes are large fat cells that store energy in a single lipid droplet. The droplet pushes the nucleus and thin cytoplasm to the rim, and clusters of these cells form the fat lobules of the hypodermis that cushion and insulate the body.
clinical: Obesity
In obesity, adipocytes enlarge and can also increase in number, so the fat stores grow.

Hair follicle.description: Each hair grows from a follicle, a tube of epidermis that sinks into the dermis. Cells in the bulb divide rapidly to form the hair shaft and root sheaths, while the dermal papilla below signals them to grow.
clinical: Hair loss from chemotherapy
Chemotherapy drugs kill the fast-dividing matrix cells in the hair bulb, so hair falls out within a few weeks of treatment (anagen effluvium).
Androgenetic alopecia
In androgenetic alopecia, androgens such as dihydrotestosterone (DHT) gradually shrink terminal follicles into fine vellus-type follicles, so hair becomes thinner and shorter over time.
Acne
Acne forms when sebaceous glands make excess sebum and the follicle opening becomes blocked, letting Cutibacterium acnes bacteria multiply.
Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is caused by faulty CFTR chloride channels, so sweat ducts reabsorb too little chloride and sweat is unusually salty. The sweat chloride test is a standard diagnostic test for it.

Vessels & nerves.description: Arterioles and venules form plexuses in the dermis and hypodermis that feed the skin, follicles and glands. Capillary loops rise into the dermal papillae to supply the living epidermis, and sensory nerves carry touch, pain and temperature signals to the spinal cord and brain.
clinical: Raynaud phenomenon
In Raynaud phenomenon, small arteries and arterioles in the fingers and toes go into spasm in cold or stress, so the skin turns white, then blue, then red as blood returns.
Shingles

Shingles occurs when varicella-zoster virus, dormant in a sensory nerve ganglion, reactivates and travels along one sensory nerve. It causes a painful blistering rash in a single band of skin, called a dermatome.

Sensory receptors.description: A Pacinian corpuscle is an onion-like receptor, about 1 to 2 mm across, made of concentric lamellae around a single nerve ending in the deep dermis and hypodermis. The lamellae filter out steady pressure, so the corpuscle responds to vibration and rapid changes in pressure, and its myelinated axon carries the signal to the spinal cord.

parts.description: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of the epidermis, made of flat, dead keratinocytes called corneocytes that have lost their nuclei and are filled with keratin. Each cell is wrapped in a tough, cross-linked protein shell called the cornified envelope, and lipid-rich layers between the cells make this layer the main barrier against water loss and microbes. Its outer cells are shed continuously as skin flakes. In a section it forms a dense pink band at the surface, with no nuclei visible.

The stratum granulosum is the layer of flattened keratinocytes lying just beneath the stratum corneum, usually only a few cells thick. Its cells are packed with coarse, dark basophilic keratohyalin granules and release lamellar bodies that secrete lipids to seal the skin barrier, and their nuclei and organelles break down as they die. Tight junctions form here, and filaggrin gene mutations cause ichthyosis vulgaris, a dry scaling skin disorder. In a section, look for the flattened cells with dark granules just under the surface.

The stratum spinosum, or prickle-cell layer, is the thick middle layer of the epidermis, lying above the stratum basale and made of several rows of polyhedral keratinocytes. Neighbouring cells are joined by many desmosomes, and fixation shrinks the cell junctions into spiny 'prickles' that help identify the layer in a section. The cells are rich in keratin filaments, and Langerhans cells, which present antigens to immune cells, live among them. In pemphigus vulgaris, autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 split this layer.

The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis, a single row of cuboidal to low columnar keratinocytes resting on the basement membrane. These are the stem and dividing cells that renew the epidermis, and they are anchored to the basement membrane by hemidesmosomes. In a section, look for the one row of small, dark-nucleated cells lining the epidermis along the wavy border with the dermal papillae.

The papillary dermis is the thin, upper layer of the dermis, made of loose connective tissue with fine type I and III collagen fibrils and many fibroblasts. Its finger-like dermal papillae interlock with the epidermal rete ridges to resist shearing, and its capillary loops nourish the avascular epidermis by diffusion. In a section, look for the finely textured connective tissue just beneath the epidermis, with capillary loops in the papillae.

The reticular dermis is the deep, thick layer of the dermis, lying beneath the papillary dermis and merging with the hypodermis below. It is made of dense irregular connective tissue rich in type I collagen, which gives the skin its strength and stretch resistance, and it houses the hair follicles, sweat glands, larger vessels and nerves. In a section, look for thick, coarse collagen bundles interwoven in many directions.

keys: Hypodermis fibrous septa – tissue restoration cover
parts.description: The fibrous septa of the hypodermis are the bands of dense collagen that run through the fat and divide it into lobules. They are continuous above with the reticular dermis and below with the deep fascia, tethering the skin in place, and they carry the larger blood vessels and nerves that supply the skin. In a section they show as pink, fibrous strands with small vessels running between the pale fat lobules.

keys: Adipose lobules – bulk continuity – tissue restoration cover
parts.description: Adipose lobules are the compartments of white fat in the hypodermis, each made of a cluster of adipocytes (fat cells) served by a rich capillary network. Fibrous septa surround each lobule and separate it from its neighbours, and each fat cell stores energy in a single large lipid droplet. In a section, the lobules show as a honeycomb of clear, empty-looking fat cells, with each nucleus pushed to the edge of its cell.

Keratinocyte nuclei are the nuclei of the epidermal keratinocytes, the cells that make up most of the epidermis. They are round to oval and stain blue-purple with haematoxylin, and they are present in the basal, spinous and granular layers. The nuclei break down as cells die near the top of the granular layer, so none remain in the stratum corneum. In a section, the point where nuclei vanish marks the boundary between living and dead epidermis.

Keratohyalin granules are the coarse, dark, irregular granules in the cytoplasm of keratinocytes in the stratum granulosum. They are made mainly of two proteins, profilaggrin and loricrin: profilaggrin is broken down into filaggrin, which clumps keratin filaments together, while loricrin helps build the tough cornified envelope, the protein shell under each cell's membrane. In a section they show as dense, basophilic clumps in the upper living cells, just below the stratum corneum.

keys: Melanocyte soma and dendrites – restoration cover
parts.description: Melanocytes are the pigment-making cells of the epidermis, found in the stratum basale among the basal keratinocytes. The melanocyte soma is the cell body, from which long dendrites reach between keratinocytes and pass melanin-filled melanosomes to them, forming the epidermal melanin unit that shades nuclei against UV light. In routine haematoxylin and eosin sections the cell body shows as a clear halo among the basal cells, and the dendrites are seen best with DOPA or silver stains.

The melanocyte nucleus is the nucleus of the melanocyte, the pigment-producing cell that sits in the stratum basale between basal keratinocytes. It is usually round to oval and lies within a clear cytoplasmic halo, a feature that helps tell melanocytes apart from keratinocytes in a section. The melanosomes made in this cell are passed to neighbouring keratinocytes, where the melanin forms a protective cap over their nuclei.

The melanocyte nucleus is the nucleus of a melanocyte, the pigment-producing cell that lies in the basal layer of the epidermis among the basal keratinocytes. It is round and usually paler than the neighbouring basal nuclei, which helps tell melanocytes apart from keratinocytes. The melanocyte's long dendrites pass packets of melanin (melanosomes) to surrounding keratinocytes, so each nucleus sits at the centre of one epidermal melanin unit, the melanocyte and the keratinocytes it supplies.

An adipose lobule is a rounded cluster of fat cells (adipocytes) that forms one unit of the hypodermis. Thin fibrous septa, which carry the blood vessels and nerves, separate each lobule from its neighbours. In a section, a lobule shows a mass of pale, empty-looking fat cells, and the lobules together cushion and insulate the body.

The peripheral cytoplasm of an adipocyte is the thin rim of cytoplasm that lies between the large lipid droplet and the cell membrane. The cell's organelles, such as the energy-making mitochondria, are squeezed into this narrow layer. In haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections it appears as a thin, pale crescent around the droplet, and together with the flattened nucleus it gives the fat cell its characteristic signet-ring look.

The adipocyte lipid droplet is the single large fat droplet that fills most of an adipocyte, the white fat cell, and stores triglyceride as an energy reserve. When the body needs energy, hormones such as adrenaline trigger lipolysis, which breaks the droplet down and releases fatty acids into the blood. Because processing solvents dissolve the fat, the droplet appears as an empty, clear space in haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections.

An adipocyte's peripheral nucleus is the flattened nucleus of the fat cell, pushed to the edge of the cell by the lipid droplet. Because the droplet fills almost the whole cell, the nucleus is squeezed into a thin crescent against the cell membrane rather than sitting in the centre. In a section of the hypodermis, look for a small, darkly stained nucleus pressed against the rim of each empty fat cell.

The hair shaft is the column of dead, keratinised cells (filled with the tough protein keratin) that forms the hair itself and projects above the skin surface. Its outer cuticle is a layer of overlapping scales pointing towards the tip, the cortex (the bulk of the shaft) holds the melanin pigment, and a central core called the medulla may be absent. In the axilla, pubis and beard, fine downy (vellus) hairs are converted into coarser terminal hairs at puberty by androgens (sex hormones).

The inner root sheath is a temporary epithelial layer that wraps the growing hair shaft inside the follicle, lying between the hair and the outer root sheath. It has three layers: Henle's layer on the outside, Huxley's layer (which contains trichohyalin granules, a hardening protein) and an inner sheath cuticle of overlapping scales that interlocks with the hair cuticle. It moulds and guides the hair as it grows, then breaks down at the level of the sebaceous duct opening, so it never reaches the surface.

The outer root sheath is the downward continuation of the epidermis that surrounds the hair follicle from the surface to the bulb. Below the isthmus (the narrow middle part of the follicle), its cells are pale, glycogen-rich (packed with a stored sugar) and do not keratinise. The bulge, where the arrector pili muscle attaches, holds the follicle's stem cells, which regenerate the follicle in each cycle and help repair the epidermis after injury.

The hair bulb (matrix) is the expanded, onion-shaped base of a growing (anagen) hair, sitting in the lower dermis and hypodermis and cupped over the dermal papilla. Its matrix cells divide very rapidly to form the hair shaft and the inner root sheath, and melanocytes within the matrix pass pigment to the growing cortex. Because these cells divide so fast, anti-cancer drugs commonly cause hair loss (anagen effluvium).

The dermal papilla of the hair is a small knot of specialised fibroblasts and capillaries that sits inside the base of the hair bulb, attached by a narrow stalk to the connective tissue sheath of the follicle. It sends signals that tell the matrix cells to divide, so its size influences the thickness of the hair. The papilla shrinks as follicles miniaturise in androgenetic alopecia (male- or female-pattern hair loss).

The sebaceous gland is a lobulated holocrine gland (its whole cell is shed as secretion) lying in the angle between the hair follicle and the arrector pili muscle. Basal cells at the edge of each lobule divide and move inwards, filling with lipid until they break down to form sebum. The sebum drains through a short duct into the follicle at the isthmus (the narrow middle part of the follicle). Androgens enlarge the glands at puberty, and blockage of the pilosebaceous unit (the follicle and its gland) causes acne.

The arrector pili muscle is a small slip of smooth muscle that runs obliquely from the bulge of a hair follicle up to the papillary dermis (the upper layer of the dermis). When it contracts it pulls the follicle upright, producing 'goose bumps' (cutis anserina), and it squeezes sebum out of the adjacent sebaceous gland. Its sympathetic (adrenergic) nerve supply makes it contract in cold or when frightened.

Arterioles are small muscular arteries that carry oxygenated blood from the deeper plexus of the dermis and hypodermis into the capillaries that supply the skin, hair follicles and glands. Their smooth-muscle wall is controlled by sympathetic nerves, so arterioles can narrow or widen to regulate skin blood flow and body temperature. In a section, look for round vessels with a muscular wall that is thick relative to a small lumen, unlike the thin-walled venules.

Venules are the small vessels that collect blood from the capillary beds and drain it towards the veins. In the skin they gather into the subpapillary venous plexus, a network just beneath the papillary dermis. Their walls are thin with few smooth-muscle cells, and they are usually wider than arterioles. Postcapillary venules are also the main site where white blood cells leave the circulation during inflammation.

The subpapillary plexus is the horizontal network of small vessels that lies just below the dermal papillae, at the junction of the papillary and reticular dermis. It is fed by ascending arterioles from the deeper plexus and gives rise to the capillary loops that rise into the papillae. In a section, it appears as a band of vessels running parallel to the skin surface, and dilated vessels here help release body heat.

Papillary capillary loops are the hairpin-shaped capillaries that rise up into the dermal papillae from the subpapillary plexus. Their thin endothelial walls allow oxygen and nutrients to pass into the epidermis, which has no blood vessels of its own and depends on this diffusion for nourishment. In a section, the loops appear as small profiles packed with red blood cells within the dermal papillae, close to the epidermis.

The cutaneous nerve and its branches are the peripheral nerve trunks that run through the reticular dermis and hypodermis to supply the skin. They carry sensory fibres from touch, pain and temperature receptors, and autonomic fibres for blood vessels, sweat glands and arrector pili muscles. In a section, a nerve appears as bundles of fibres (fascicles), each wrapped in a tough sheath called the perineurium, and its branches fan out towards the epidermis.

Free nerve endings are the bare, unencapsulated terminal branches of sensory axons that lie between the cells of the epidermis and dermis. They detect pain, temperature, itch and crude touch, and their terminal branches are unmyelinated. In routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections they are very hard to see, so they are identified with silver stains or with immunostaining for PGP 9.5, a general nerve marker.

Hair follicle nerve endings are the sensory receptors that wrap around the lower part of each hair follicle and detect movement of the hair. The typical receptor is the lanceolate (lance-shaped) ending, in which myelinated axons form flattened terminals that spiral around the follicle and respond when the hair is bent. In a section, the endings appear as spiral or ring-like fibres encircling the follicle in its lower part.

The Pacinian corpuscle is a large, onion-shaped, encapsulated mechanoreceptor, about 1 mm long, that lies in the deep dermis and hypodermis. Its concentric lamellae are layers of flattened cells surrounding a central nerve terminal, and they act as a filter that lets rapid changes in pressure or vibration reach the nerve while blocking steady pressure. In routine sections, its layered, onion-skin pattern around a central core makes it easy to recognise.

The Pacinian axon terminal is the bare, unmyelinated tip of a sensory axon at the centre of a Pacinian corpuscle. The myelin sheath is lost as the axon enters the inner core, and the terminal is squeezed by the lamellae whenever the corpuscle is deformed. This mechanical deformation opens stretch-sensitive ion channels in the terminal membrane, which generates the nerve impulse that travels to the spinal cord.

The secretory coil of the eccrine sweat gland is the coiled tubular part, lying in the deep dermis or upper hypodermis, that makes sweat. Clear cells secrete a watery fluid with the same salt concentration as blood plasma, dark cells secrete glycoproteins (sugar-protein molecules), and myoepithelial (contractile, muscle-like) cells beneath them squeeze the sweat into the duct. In a section, clear cells look pale and dark cells stain more intensely. Sympathetic cholinergic nerves (which release acetylcholine) supply the gland, and sweating is the body's main way of losing heat.

The eccrine sweat duct carries sweat from the secretory coil to the skin surface. Its two layers of small, dark cuboidal cells reabsorb sodium and chloride through channels (ENaC for sodium, CFTR for chloride), so surface sweat is hypotonic (less salty than blood). In cystic fibrosis, a faulty CFTR channel leaves sweat salty, which is the basis of the sweat test. The duct enters the epidermis at the tip of a rete ridge (a downward epidermal peg) and spirals through it (the acrosyringium) to open at a sweat pore.
